notes.lines: Every precinct line is the Texas Legislative Council's, generalised by at most 1.5 metres and set on a grid of 0.00001 degree (about a metre). A point within a few metres of a line can fall on either side of it.
notes.precincts: A shape is a county election precinct as the county reported it to the Texas Legislative Council for the March 3, 2026 primary, the newest statewide file. A county may have changed a precinct since; the county elections office is the authority on which precinct an address is in.
notes.districts: Each precinct's congressional, State House, State Senate and State Board of Education district is the Council's own table for the 2026 elections. State law (Election Code 42.005) keeps every precinct wholly inside one district of each. The congressional districts are the plan enacted in 2025 (PLANC2333), in effect for 2026: they differ from the districts of 2024, and no reader is placed by the old lines. The State House and Senate districts are the plans the Census Bureau's 2024 files also carry, block for block.
notes.places: Texas's cities, towns and villages, by the Census Bureau's 2025 lines. A precinct's mcd is the place holding half or more of it (absent outside every one); mcd_all lists every place it reaches where it reaches more than one or lies partly outside: to say which place a point is in, ask the mcd layer, not the precinct.
notes.commissioners: Commissioners precincts are drawn for Bastrop County, Bell County, Bexar County, Brazos County, Collin County, Comal County, Dallas County, Denton County, Fort Bend County, Harris County, Hays County, Hidalgo County, Lubbock County, Montgomery County, Tarrant County, Travis County, Williamson County, each from the county's own lines. Every other county's commissioner contests are listed under check, with the reason. Texas law keeps every election precinct wholly inside one commissioners precinct.
notes.justice: Justice of the peace precincts are named by the precincts of Bell County, Bexar County, Brazos County, Collin County, Dallas County, Denton County, Harris County, Hays County, Lubbock County, Montgomery County, Tarrant County, Travis County, each from the county's own lines; constables are elected from the same precincts. Elsewhere those contests are placed on the county.
notes.courts: District court judges are elected by judicial districts of whole counties, which overlap (one county can be in many), so no judicial district is drawn: each district court contest is placed by the counties the ballot list ties it to. Courts of appeals districts are whole counties (Government Code 22.201); coa and coa2 name a precinct's, and coa15 the Fifteenth, which is the whole state.
notes.school: School district lines are the Census Bureau's 2025 file. Which districts a precinct lies in is analysis, not an official list: a district counts when its part of the precinct is at least 60 metres thick somewhere; school_pct is each district's share of the precinct (land and water, not voters).
notes.polling: Texas publishes no statewide list of polling places that a script may read; the county elections office is the authority.
notes.authority: For which precinct and districts an address is in, and where to vote, the county elections office and the Secretary of State's voter portal are the authority.
notes.precinct_ids: A precinct's id is its county's five digits, a full stop and the county's own precinct number as the Council gives it (48201.0123 is Harris County precinct 0123).
